findings.note: Two caveats on the negative. The filter is a literal substring match on ERROR, so lines using a different severity token (Err, SEVERE, level=error lowercase, or MongoDB's own 'E' severity letter in its structured format) would not have matched — a case-insensitive or severity-field query is worth running before treating this as conclusive. Also, if the container was killed abruptly, final log lines may never have been flushed to Loki. This result constrains mongodb-rate's own logs only; it says nothing about errors recorded by callers, the kubelet, or control-plane events, which are where the cause of an unannounced termination would more likely appear.

No error-severity line naming a configuration value or an injected fault exists in mongodb-rate's own logs for this window — the pod logged nothing at ERROR level at all, including in the moments around termination.

ruled_out.why: The substring filter for ERROR returned zero lines over the window containing the termination, so no such line was emitted by this pod.
ruled_out.hypothesis: mongodb-rate logged an explicit error identifying a bad config parameter or a deliberately injected fault just before it died.

ruled_out.why: An application that detects its own fatal condition normally logs at error severity first; the absence of any ERROR line is inconsistent with a self-reported shutdown and points toward an abrupt external kill (OOM, SIGKILL, node/container-level eviction) that left no application log trail.
ruled_out.hypothesis: The termination was a graceful, self-diagnosed application-level failure that the process announced before exiting.

ruled_out.why: The window starts ~29 minutes before termination and contains no ERROR lines, so there was no gradual error accumulation visible in this pod's logs.
ruled_out.hypothesis: A sustained pre-termination error storm (repeated connection, auth, or storage failures) degraded the pod over the preceding half hour.

verdict.reasoning: Three independent log cuts agree the process was healthy at the storage layer and died to an external signal with no self-reported error, which excludes OOM/segfault (handled SIGTERM path), disk_fill and datastore_corruption (clean recovery, checkpoint, no space or parse errors), and bad_deploy (engine config byte-identical across both starts, first creation rather than a rolling update). The change log places an automation-authored fault-injection-named ConfigMap seconds before the container started, which is evidence for a deliberately induced stop of the process rather than a wrong configuration value doing work in the request path. Remediation is to bring the process back and keep it running (remove the injected kill and restart the workload).
verdict.root_cause: mongodb-rate's pod was created fresh at ~15:01 by platform-automation and then terminated externally by SIGTERM (kill(2) from pid 0/uid 0) within seconds, twice: two clean WiredTiger startup cycles at 15:01:02 and 15:01:04 each ended in signal-handler-driven orderly shutdown, the last at 15:01:10 [tr_9948fd3a2026][tr_fcd9d6881852]. The service itself logged no errors and its storage engine opened, recovered and checkpointed cleanly, so neither corruption, disk, nor storage misconfiguration is the mechanism [tr_fcd9d6881852][tr_4d3c551d555b]. The change set is a first-time workload creation accompanied by a ConfigMap whose name indicates fault-injection/failure-administration intent, landing seconds before the container came up [tr_616998c15f26]. The best-supported reading is an injected/administered kill of the mongodb-rate process: the datastore is absent from the topology while its socket/endpoint churns, leaving callers in the hotel-reservation namespace without a rate datastore. With no metrics available for this service at all [tr_596c016954c3], the mechanism is the process being stopped/killed rather than any value being wrong.

alternatives.why_not: Both engine opens succeeded against a mounted, readable data path with clean journal recovery, so no storage configuration value was actually wrong at the point of failure [tr_fcd9d6881852].
alternatives.root_cause: The PVC rate-pvc was created and updated twice within seconds, and the resulting volume rebind forced the pod to be torn down and rescheduled repeatedly.

alternatives.why_not: The teardown follows the handled SIGTERM path with a full ordered shutdown and only 3 in-flight operations interrupted; an OOM kill would be SIGKILL with no such sequence [tr_9948fd3a2026].
alternatives.root_cause: A lowered memory limit on the newly created workload caused the container runtime to terminate mongodb repeatedly.

open_questions: Whether the SIGTERM came from the fault-injection ConfigMap, normal Kubernetes pod lifecycle/rescheduling during first creation, or a liveness-probe failure - no kubelet or pod-event evidence was gathered.
Whether mongodb-rate stayed down after 15:01:10 or recovered; the log window ends at 15:02:30 and no post-onset startup was observed.
Which callers (e.g. rate service) actually degraded, and whether they hung to deadline or failed fast - no upstream metrics or logs were dispatched.
What alert fired at 15:02:21 and on what signal, given Prometheus holds no series for this service [tr_596c016954c3].

draft.title: mongodb-rate: pod created, then stopped from outside within seconds

sections.body: The page named a single service, mongodb-rate, at warning severity, with a blast radius of one and no upstream or downstream edge implicated. There was no graph anchor to start from — the datastore does not appear in the service topology that the tooling draws, so the usual "walk the callers" move was unavailable from the first minute. The practical consequence for the responder: everything below was reconstructed from the pod's own logs and the change log, because neither traces nor metrics existed for this service. If you pick this record up months later, start where we ended up starting: Loki, pod selector on the hotel-reservation namespace.
sections.heading: What the page looked like

sections.body: Working backwards from the page (call it T+0), the whole story sits in a roughly twenty-second band about a minute and a half earlier. At about T-90s the platform automation created the workload for the first time — container, Service, two ConfigMaps, and a PersistentVolumeClaim. At about T-79s the storage engine opened cleanly: sub-second open, recovery timestamps established, journal recovery run to completion, no table-logging rewrites. Seconds later the process was shut down in an orderly, signal-driven way. At about T-77s the identical cycle repeated — same engine configuration string, byte for byte — and ended the same way. At roughly T-71s the process logged receipt of signal 15, attributed to kill(2) from pid 0/uid 0, then walked the full teardown: replication coordinator stepped down, listening sockets closed, unix socket file removed, storage engine, checkpoint, journal and session-sweeper threads shut down. Only three in-flight operations were interrupted, so the instance was carrying essentially no load when it was stopped. The log window we queried runs out shortly after the page, so there is no observation of whether a third startup followed.
sections.heading: Reconstructed order of events

sections.body: All seven recorded changes to this service cluster into that same twenty-second span and all carry the platform-automation actor, not a human. The entries describe first-time creation rather than modification of something already running. The PersistentVolumeClaim (rate-pvc) was created and then updated twice inside about seven seconds — the only object touched after its initial create, which made it the natural first suspect. One of the two ConfigMaps carries a name that advertises deliberate failure-administration tooling aimed at this service, and it landed seconds before the container came up. Searching the full preceding 24 hours turned up nothing at all before that burst: no older edit, no drift, no scaling or replica-count action, no image roll.
sections.heading: What the change log said, and what it did not

sections.body:
Storage was the loudest-looking lead and it went nowhere. The PVC being rewritten twice reads like a volume problem, but both engine opens succeeded against the data path, read the journal and completed recovery — which cannot happen on an unmounted or unreadable volume. No salvage, no repair, no corruption markers; the closes wrote checkpoints cleanly. The engine configuration string was identical across both startups, so there was no storage-level config drift hiding behind the PVC edits.

Crash theories also failed. An out-of-memory kill or a segfault leaves no orderly teardown; what we have is a handled termination path with clean-shutdown marking, so the process did not die of its own accord. A separate pass filtering for ERROR-severity lines across the full half-hour window returned nothing — not one line, including around the stop. That empty answer cuts both ways: it rules out an error storm building over the preceding half hour and rules out a self-diagnosed fatal condition, but it is also why we never got an application-level statement of what hit it.

One timing argument we entertained and should flag as misleading: because the termination sits near the end of the queried window, it is tempting to say it post-dates onset and therefore cannot be the trigger. Given the page itself landed about a minute after, and given the broad log pull was marked truncated (quieter pre-event lines may exist and simply were not returned), that reasoning is weaker than it looks. Do not lean on it.

Finally, the metrics path is a dead end by construction, not by accident. Error-ratio, p95, request rate, and resource series all came back with nothing over both the incident window and the preceding baseline. This is an unavailable result, not a zero — the backend holds no span-derived series for this service because it emits no traces that become metrics. Re-running the same templates with a different range will not help, and nobody should read the blank chart as evidence the datastore was healthy.
sections.heading: Dead ends worth keeping

sections.body: The best-supported reading is that mongodb-rate was stopped from outside, twice, within seconds of each fresh start, by an administered SIGTERM. The service itself logged no errors; its storage engine opened, recovered and checkpointed correctly every time. The mechanism is the process being stopped, not any value being wrong. Downstream, the datastore is absent from the topology while its socket and endpoint churn, which leaves callers in the hotel-reservation namespace without a rate datastore. The co-located ConfigMap named for failure administration is the obvious candidate for who sent the signal, but we never closed that loop. Confidence is low. The indicated remedy class is a restart.
sections.heading: Where we landed

sections.body:
Nobody pulled kubelet output or pod lifecycle events, so the source of the SIGTERM is unproven: it could be the administration ConfigMap, ordinary Kubernetes rescheduling during a first creation, or a liveness probe failing and the kubelet reaping the container. That is the single highest-value gap.

We also do not know whether the service stayed down after the last stop — the log window ends about a minute past the page with no later startup observed. Extend the window first thing.

No upstream metrics or logs were ever dispatched, so we cannot say which callers (the rate service being the obvious one) actually degraded, or whether they hung to their deadline versus failed fast.

And it remains unclear what signal the page itself fired on, given the metrics store holds no series for this service at all. Whatever fired it came from somewhere other than the place we looked.
sections.heading: Still open — do these next time

proposal.risk: Abstaining leaves the rate datastore down if it never came back, so hotel-reservation callers keep failing. Restarting instead would risk recreating a container that the still-active external killer terminates again, masking the real cause and burning the one-shot (irreversible) restart while confidence is low.
proposal.if_wrong: If a Loki query past 15:02:30 shows mongodb-rate still absent or looping startup/SIGTERM, and a kubelet/pod-event check shows no external killer still active, then restart_service becomes justified and this abstention was too cautious. Conversely, if pod events name the fault-injection ConfigMap as the killer, a restart would be re-killed and the fix lies outside this system.
proposal.blast_radius: No one sees a change now. Any later restart touches mongodb-rate only, with callers in the hotel-reservation namespace (the rate service) seeing connection resets during recreate.
proposal.expected_effect: No action taken, so nothing changes. A restart would only be verifiable if a post-restart mongod startup in Loki were NOT followed within ~10s by a SignalHandler shutdown - but we never saw whether mongodb-rate recovered after 15:01:10 (log window ends 15:02:30), and no metrics exist for this service, so the effect is currently unobservable.
